title: Former AMP boss part of big plans at Zurich
full_text:
International insurance heavyweight Zurich has recruited former AMP boss Alexis George to its board as part of a fresh assault on the Australian market writing general and life insurance.
Until January this year, Ms George ran AMP and is a career banker. She replaced former Suncorp boss John Mulcahy.
She has brought her “experience of transformation” to Zurich, after presiding over a turbulent period at AMP when the financial giant sold off a number of key operations: AMP Life, AMP Capital, and much of its financial advice arm.
Despite entering the Australian market in 1961, Zurich trails incumbent players Suncorp, QBE, Allianz, and IAG in the general insurance market. It has largely competed in more niche parts of the local insurance market, where returns can be higher.
It will hold nearly $5.5bn in gross written premium by the end of the year, almost $1bn higher after recent acquisitions. It is pushing into general insurance and making an advance on the potentially lucrative life insurance market within regulated superannuation.
Zurich chair and former regulator Geoff Summerhayes said he hoped to see the insurer grow to a top-five commercial provider in Australia within years. “We can see a pathway to doing that,” he said.
Mr Summerhayes, who also chairs Mercer Investments Australia, was also a member of APRA for five years. He was there when Zurich’s local operation was a “flag on the map” – small and barely recognisable.
Five years ago, Zurich’s two arms operated as distinct businesses: a travel insurer and a motor insurer. But Mr Summerhayes said under Zurich’s current leadership, headed by Justin Delaney, it added ClearView’s life insurance arm and pushed into general insurance through a deal with financial player Honey.
Zurich bought ClearView in July for $415m. IAG’s buyout of RACQ, which previously underwrote Honey policies, will see Zurich assume its place from October.
Zurich’s arrangements with Clearview and Honey Insurance are important to framing its future in Australia, and it was important that both are “digestible”, Ms George said.
“There’s many scars on people’s backs around that,” she said with a nod to when acquisitions go wrong.
Mr Summerhayes said Zurich had repositioned itself as a general insurer, getting out of “some of the bigger risks that we were uncomfortable with”.
Despite the otherwise gloomy prospects for Australia’s economic growth, insurance was essential to businesses. “The risk is not going away,” he said.
Mr Summerhayes pointed to Zurich’s life insurance division, which is targeting superannuation providers over the more traditional model of selling to those receiving financial advice.
Much of the advised life insurance market has fallen away in the wake of the 2018 Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry.
Mr Summerhayes agreed the “model needs to change”.
“The shame about what has happened is advice now falls into the category of the high net wealth and wealth. Advice for the middle market in a retail personal sense is out of some people’s reach,” he said.
“We are a believer in advice and think it’s important but there’s a reason why we’re growing our group insurance business.” Insurers have slugged Australians with major premium price rises in recent years as the cost of insuring homes and cars has soared. IAG and Suncorp, the two biggest players in the market, have also been fending off entrants like Budget Direct, owned by Auto & General, and Youi, owned by the South African player OUTsurance Group.
